Spot-winged antbird (Myrmelastes leucostigma) is a medium-sized antbird inhabiting the understory of lowland terra firme forests across the western Amazon basin. Field studies of this species have documented that eggs are incubated at approximately 38 °C [T = 38 °C], and hatching occurs after an incubation period of roughly 15 days [ab = roughly 15 days]. Newly emerged altricial nestlings have a mass at hatching of approximately 3.9 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.9 grams], a value inferred from closely related congeners. This initial body mass is relatively modest among thamnophilids, reflecting the species' typical investment in a small clutch size and protracted parental care. The nestlings are brooded intensively for the first week, with the female providing most of the thermal regulation while the male delivers arthropod prey. As the feather-growing nestling develops, its caloric demands increase substantially, requiring frequent provisioning visits from both parents. The pair maintains a stable nest environment throughout this critical period, and the developmental trajectory appears tightly linked to local prey abundance in the forest understory.

During the active metabolic phase characteristic of adults in the genus Myrmelastes, body temperature is typically maintained at around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], representing the thermal regime at which key life-history events have been measured. Under these conditions, the nestling period culminates in fledging, with young birds achieving their first flight at approximately 13.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 13.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This post-hatching fledging interval is comparable to values reported for other obligate ant-following antbirds, reflecting the selective pressures of a foraging guild that requires early mobility to follow mobile prey swarms. Following fledging, the paternal-fed chick remains dependent on adult caregivers for several additional weeks, during which flight feather maturation continues and foraging skills develop gradually. The post-fledging period is energetically demanding, and mortality during this transitional phase is thought to be substantial, although precise rates have not been quantified for this species. Brood parasitism and predation pressures further shape the timing of nest departure.

Continuing under the thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that define the species' active metabolic state, sexual maturation is a relatively rapid process in this species compared to larger thamnophilids. Puberty, defined as the attainment of fully developed gonads capable of gamete production, occurs at approximately 40.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 40.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively early onset of reproductive capacity suggests that individuals may attempt breeding in their first year of life, provided that suitable territories and mates are available. The attainment of reproductive maturity coincides with the completion of skeletal growth and the achievement of adult plumage, which in males is characterized by a slate-gray body with diagnostic white spots on the wing coverts. Females, which reach a smaller adult size, exhibit a warmer brown coloration with similar wing spotting. The timing of gonadal activation is likely influenced by photoperiod and rainfall patterns, which in the western Amazon are relatively aseasonal, permitting year-round breeding opportunities in some years.

Adult body mass exhibits modest sexual size dimorphism in this species, with mature females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 24 grams [Wwi = 24 grams] and males attaining a slightly larger ultimate wet weight of 26 grams [Wwi = 26 grams]. This mass difference is typical of many antbirds in which males are marginally heavier, possibly reflecting the energetic demands of territorial defense and song production. The adult body mass is sustained through a diet composed primarily of orthopterans, spiders, and other arthropods flushed by army ant swarms, which the birds follow as professional ant-followers. The basal metabolic rate, measured via open-flow respirometry on resting adults at thermoneutrality, corresponds to a resting oxygen consumption of approximately 32.2 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 32.2 milliliters per hour] when measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This mass-specific metabolic rate is consistent with values predicted for a 24-gram passerine and reflects the relatively energetically expensive lifestyle of an active understory insectivore. The species shows no evidence of torpor or metabolic depression, maintaining high metabolic rates throughout the diurnal activity period.

Reproductive output in the Spot-winged antbird is comparatively low, consistent with a slow life-history strategy typical of many tropical forest passerines. Females produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and available data from congeneric species suggest that they typically raise a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This annual reproductive restraint likely reflects the energetic challenges of provisioning rapidly growing altricial nestlings in a resource-limited understory environment. The first successful breeding event typically occurs about 401 days after hatching [tR = about 401 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the time required for territory acquisition and pair formation in a saturated social at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]system. In terms of overall longevity, maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at approximately 2993 days [am = approximately 2993 days], based on tail-feather wear analysis and recapture data from banding studies conducted in undisturbed at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]lowland forest. This extended lifespan, combined with low annual fecundity and delayed first reproduction, places the Spot-winged antbird at the slow end of the life-history continuum among Neotropical passerines.
